text: Shared locks, last lesson, were about reading. This lesson covers the lock that writing takes: the exclusive lock, and it behaves very differently.

Any INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE takes an exclusive, or X, lock on the rows it changes. Exclusive means exactly that: only one transaction can hold an X lock on a given resource at a time, and left open on purpose here is Session A's UPDATE against a single product row.

Here's the key difference from a shared lock. A shared lock only conflicted with exclusive locks — other readers were fine. An exclusive lock conflicts with everything. While Session A holds it, Session B's plain SELECT blocks, and so does Session C's UPDATE against that same row. A writer blocks readers AND other writers.
And that's correct, necessary behavior. If two sessions could write the same row at once, whichever write finished last would silently overwrite the other, with no error, no warning.

Exclusive locks are also held longer than shared locks — all the way to COMMIT or ROLLBACK, not released as soon as the individual statement finishes. That's exactly why keeping transactions short matters: the longer the X lock stays held, the longer everyone else waits.

In sys.dm_tran_locks, this shows up as request_mode equal to X, with a request_status of GRANT for the holder and WAIT for anyone blocked behind it. Next up: update locks — the one that exists specifically to prevent a classic deadlock between two transactions both trying to update the same row.
